own_scenes.desc: El imperio de Berry Gordy fue un fenómeno de capitalismo negro, pero en los setenta solo sobrevivieron los artistas que escribían su material (Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, Smokey Robinson, Michael Jackson). Norman Whitfield, que pasó de chupatintas a productor, le dio un filo más áspero («I Heard It Through the Grapevine» de Gladys Knight) y, mientras Sly arrasaba en 1968, cambió el sonido de los Temptations: temas largos con guitarras rockeras, efectos espaciales, drogas («Cloud Nine», «Psychedelic Shack», «Ball of Confusion») y orgullo negro, ropa a lo Hendrix y, al final, «Papa Was a Rollin’ Stone» (1972), soul con mensaje. La huella de P-Funk era clara (Eddie Hazel y Billy Nelson tocan en «Shakey Ground»); Whitfield convirtió a los Undisputed Truth en una banda de black rock pintada de plata. Los músicos de sesión, los Funk Brothers, trabajaban en la sombra: el bajista James Jamerson, que sacaba líneas de cómo hablaba o caminaba la gente, influyó a todos. Cuando Motown se mudó a Los Ángeles, la banda se quedó en Detroit y la magia se perdió.

refs.q: One in-house writer named Norman Whitfield took some chances with the Motown formula that paid off huge funk dividends
refs.para: One in-house writer named Norman Whitfield took some chances with the Motown formula that paid off huge funk dividends for Motown records, particularly with the Temptations. Working his way up from paper pusher to producer at the label, Norman Whitfield injected a rougher edge into Motown’s hit machine, an edge that can be heard on the Temptations’ “Ain’t Too Proud to Beg,” “Can’t Get Next to You,” and clearly on Gladys Knight’s rendition of “I Heard It Through the Grapevine.” In 1968, as Sly and the Family Stone was scorching the charts, Whitfield completely changed the Temptations’ sound and recorded wild, extended songs and topical themes such as “Psychedelic Shack,” “Ball of Confusion,” and “Cloud Nine.” There were rock-style guitars, spacey sound effects, and references to psychedelic drugs. The George Clinton, Sly Stone, and Jimi Hendrix influences were obvious, as was the drug-oriented subject matter. Temptations’ lead singer Eddie Kendricks can be heard on “Take a Stroll Through Your Mind” singing “one drag was all it took/and I was hooked.” The chorus to the Temptations’ No. 2 pop hit “Cloud Nine” went, “I’m doing fine/on cloud nine.” Perhaps even more significant was the strident black pride themes, heard on tunes like “Message from a Black Man,” and “Slave.”

refs.q: Bassist James Jamerson was the best-known musician and had perhaps the strongest impact of any single player in the Motown family.
refs.para: Bassist James Jamerson was the best-known musician and had perhaps the strongest impact of any single player in the Motown family. His ability to cook a groove, skipping, stopping, and swinging while still hanging tight (listen to Stevie Wonder’s “For Once in My Life” or “Uptight”), influenced musicians everywhere, and made it difficult for live acts to replicate his sound. podcast.title: Blueprint for PIR
podcast.body: Motown served as the explicit and foundational blueprint for Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff when they embarked on creating their own record label, Philadelphia International Records, inspiring their business and creative model. "Motown was their blueprint."

podcast.title: Crossover Appeal Strategy
podcast.body: Motown effectively attracted a white audience by skillfully incorporating familiar pop elements into its music, while simultaneously retaining its African American following through its R&B roots and subtle gospel influences, thereby achieving broad mass appeal. "Motel was able to draw a white audience for its music because the songs had these familiar pop elements, but it also maintained its African American following because the songs were still R&B with the times a little tinge of gospel."

podcast.title: Detroit's Backbeat
podcast.body: Motown music from Detroit was renowned for its distinctive backbeat, a fundamental element of its regional sound that contributed to its widespread appeal and recognizability. "the backbeat of Detroit's Motown"

podcast.title: Local Musicians for Live Gigs – Iggy Pop's Role
podcast.body: In the mid-sixties, many Motown acts such as The Shangri-La's, The Temptations, and The Four Tops toured with only a couple of core musicians (typically a guitar and piano player). They would then hire local musicians, including bass players and drummers, to fill out the live band, rehearsing briefly before each show. Iggy Pop was one such local drummer, highly skilled at picking up songs quickly. "When a lot of the Motown acts at the time You know the Shangri-La's and the temptations and the four tops and others played live gigs They toured just with a couple of musicians usually guitar player and maybe a piano player The rest of the band including the bass player and the drummer would be hired locally."

podcast.body: Motown music is considered too energetic for dogs because its tempo does not match their resting heartbeat. "Motown to energetic."

podcast.title: Relaxed Rhythms
podcast.body: Motown music is characterized by its "relaxed rhythms," which can influence drummers like Chad Smith and contribute to their playing style. "Chad Smith, a big hard-hitting dude from Detroit who grew up listening to the relaxed rhythms of Motown."

podcast.title: Resistance to Political Messages
podcast.body: Berry Gordy, the founder and president of Motown, was strongly opposed to the inclusion of overt political messages in Motown songs, famously resisting Marvin Gaye's desire to release "What's Going On." "Barry Gordy, whose Motowns founder and president was also very resistant to political messages in Motown songs."
